utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-03-68-T, the Prosecutor versus Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Madam, and good morning to you. Mr. Oric, good morning to you and can you follow the proceedings in your own language?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour ladies and gentlemen, I can follow the proceedings in my own language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. You may sit down. Appearances for the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours my name is Jan Wubben, lead counsel for the Prosecution. Also good morning to my learned friends of the Defence. I'm here together with co-counsels, Ms. Patricia Sellers and Mr. Gramsci Di Fazio, and our case manager, Ms. Donnica Henry-Frijlink.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Wubben and good morning to you and your team. Appearances for the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour. Good morning to the colleagues from the team of the Prosecution. My name is Vasvija Vidovic and together with Mr. John Jones I appear on behalf of Mr. Naser Oric. With us are our legal assistants Ms. Adisa Mehic and our CaseMap manager. Mr. Geoff Roberts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Vidovic, and good morning to you and your team. I'm sorry to disappoint you. I tried very hard together with my staff to find another courtroom for this exercise, especially because of what your requirements are, Mr. Wubben. I have to disappoint you. We tried and tried. We even tried again this morning, but it simply won't work. So we will need to carry out the exercise here in this courtroom, which is not the ideal place for this kind of exercise. However -- yes. Yes, I recognise Mr. Wubben.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Before the submissions start, the Prosecution concedes that there is no case to answer regarding command responsibility under Article 7(3) of the Statute for wanton destruction and plunder of the hamlet of Bozici, that's a hamlet of Jezestica charged in counts 3 and 4 and mentioned in paragraph 31, 35, and 36 of the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is that all?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. And I have another submission that is in respect of the agreed facts and authenticated documents. Your Honour, this morning I contacted Defence with a view to request a Prosecution number. I receive it from Chambers, from the Registrar, that there will be a package of P numbers tomorrow but the Defence confirmed to me that they agree upon the admission of these agreed facts and authenticated documents as such.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I thank you and incidentally, Mr. Wubben. We will be requiring from you when you make your intervention tomorrow an indication of where you believe you have adduced evidence tending to prove the death of Mr. Bogdan Zivanovic, and that's for the purpose of count 1. And the cruel treatment of Miloje Obradovic, and that's in relation to count 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Yes, I will, Your Honour. -- Yes, I will include that in the submissions tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Right. I thank you very much, Mr. Wubben. For the time being we do not anticipate any other particular questions, not to be excluded but we don't anticipate we will have any further questions to ask. Yes. Now, by way of introduction, this is going to be an introduction of a couple of seconds, early next week, this coming week, this Tribunal, pursuant to the amended Rule 98 bis will be handing an oral decision as to whether the case should proceed as it is in its entirety, on the basis of the existing second amended indictment or whether it's the case of excluding one or more of the counts for the purpose of the rest of the trial. Because of that, and precisely because we are taxed by the amended Rule to possibly hear the submissions that you may have, as you know, we issued a scheduling order reserving today for submissions to be made by the Defence and tomorrow for submissions to be made by the Prosecution, and that will be the ends of the story. On Wednesday of next week, we anticipate to be able to hand down the decision. We would have been able probably to hand it down on Monday but as I said two weeks ago you have an important commitment related to your career, Mr. Jones, which the Trial Chamber respects and wants to respect to the utmost and therefore we would prefer to delay our decision until you are back on Wednesday.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'm obliged, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. And you kindly requested to take into account the concession that has been made by Mr. Wubben earlier on this morning relating to counts 3 and 4, as they relate to the village of Bozici and the Trial Chamber would like to know what your submissions are for the Rule 98 bis exercise purpose.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour. May it please Your Honour, to start I'd like to pass up a skeleton of the argument to help you follow my submissions and I have three copies for the Bench, copies for the Prosecution, and copies for the Chamber's legal officer, and in fact I have extra copies if need be. And that's really just to aid Your Honours as I go through the our submissions. Your Honours, our submission is that given the state of the evidence at the close of the Prosecution case, eight long months after the case began last October, we say that the Prosecution should have done the responsible thing and withdrawn the entire case from Your Honours and not simply Bozici, which is such an insignificant concession we have practically forgotten it was within the indictment because I don't think a single witness has mentioned it. History, I fear, will judge the Prosecutors very severely for not doing so, for not withdrawing the case and we trust and hope that Your Honours will do the right thing and dismiss this case in its entirety because this is a case which does not deserve to continue one moment longer. Now, it should not be unthinkable for a submission of no case to answer to succeed at this Tribunal. It's not unthinkable in national systems. Any judicial system worth its salt and with confidence in itself should not be afraid to dismiss a case when the Prosecution has not made out a case to answer. And I would hope that this Tribunal is no less a judicial institution and that more than ten years after the creation of the ICTY, it has enough confidence in itself to be able to stop a trial at the half time stage when in an appropriate case. And I trust Your Honours will have the courage to do that because it takes courage to end a case at the half time at the Tribunal because of the perception that this Tribunal that an acquittal in any form is a failure of justice rather than it being seen for what it is, the ultimate expression of justice for an innocent man to be freed in an appropriate case at the close of the Prosecution case. This is an application which should succeed. As this case has unfolded month after month since last October, those watching the trial must have thought to themselves, Surely there must be more to this case than that crimes were committed against Serb persons and property by unidentified perpetrators. But there isn't. Observers following this case must be scratching their heads and thinking, "Surely the Prosecution must have some proof, not simply that crimes were committed, but that as required by Article 7(3) of the Statute, the specific persons committing those crimes were Naser Oric's subordinates," but they don't have that proof. They haven't presented it. And surely, people following this trial will think, the Prosecution must have evidence that Naser Oric was told by someone of these crimes and that he did nothing. Again there has been nothing of that nature to the point where there is not a line of transcript or an exhibit that says that Naser Oric was informed that any of the crimes in the indictment had been committed by one of his subordinates. I ask Your Honours to think of that for a moment. That is a truly stunning fact. Answers must be given as to why such a case may be allowed to proceed when a basic building block of Article 7(3) liability is completely absent. We say this case has been misconceived from the start and that it should be put out of its misery now. So far, these deep flaws in the Prosecution case has been their problem but now they ask you to allow the case to go on only omitting charges relating to Bozici which, if you do, with the greatest of respect, will become your problem or your responsibility in any event. And questions will be asked as to why this case was allowed to continue past this point. So that's why I would ask Your Honours before taking that step to put the toughest, severest questions, to the Prosecution and I'll be suggesting some of the questions since of course we can't put questions to the Prosecution, which must be answered but to which there is no answer, for indeed Your Honours will have to address these questions in your reasoned decision which, as you've told us, you will be delivering as a matter of -- which will be - my apologies - a reasoned decision which natural justice requires to be reasoned. Now it's an incredibly grave matter to put a man on trial for war crimes, to take him from his family and home and accuse him before all the world of being responsible for atrocities. We've had eight months of evidence from a Prosecution team which is one of the best-equipped Prosecution teams in the world. I'm speaking of OTP generally, but in this trial we have five trial attorneys, a team of investigators, all the facilities of OTP that one could imagine, access to every archive potentially in the world, the right to demand cooperation from every witness in the field, with the clout of being OTP behind -- behind them, and so they should now be able to answer your questions very specifically and not with vague assertions, generalities, possibilities, inferences, but with concrete evidence. And here are some of the questions they must answer: Where is the evidence that Oric's subordinates, people under his effective control, committed the crimes charged in the indictment? Not just that people committed crimes, civilians, displaced persons, fighters, but Oric's subordinates. There is not a tittle of such evidence. All the evidence has been of unidentified perpetrators with one or two exceptions which I will deal with. Where is the evidence that Oric knew or had specific information that his subordinates had committed crimes? I would ask Your Honours to put those questions to the Prosecution. There is none. There is no evidence. And where is the evidence that Oric did not take measures open to him to prevent or punish crimes committed by his subordinates? There the uncontradicted Prosecution evidence establishes that as regards plunder and wanton destruction by civilians, no army, no authority, nobody, could stop it. Isn't that an appropriate case for dismissal at half time of those charges? I would ask how can the Prosecution even maintain this case with a straight face when its own uncontradicted evidence of its own witnesses is that Naser Oric could do nothing to prevent these crimes? And more fundamentally one's moral conscience cries out for an answer to this question which I posed in my opening speech: How can it be criminal for poor, desperate, starving civilians to steal food to feed themselves and their children? Because that's been the evidence of the Prosecution. I know I would do it, I believe Your Honours would do it, I think any decent human being would steal food to feed their starving children and wives and themselves. The Prosecution may require people to starve or be judged criminals but Your Honours should not do so. And we will be saying that plunder as charged in the indictment is nothing more than people doing what they can to survive. And we say that it's shameful particularly for the West which so spectacularly failed the people of Srebrenica to turn around and call those who stole bread and livestock criminals. And if it's wrong to condemn civilians for stealing, then how can it possibly be right to hold Oric responsible, criminally responsible, for those acts? Another question which the Prosecution must answer: Where is the evidence that Oric aided and abetted or encouraged burning and looting? The only evidence has been the opposite. The absolute opposite. That he fiercely opposed it. So this is by way of opening obviously, in our submission the Prosecution must give you clear-cut, convincing answers to these questions or the case must end here. And they will not be able to answer those questions. Therefore for them to seek to continue to prosecute this case rather than dropping it themselves is, we say, a scandal. As I say history will judge the continued Prosecution of this case very harshly, to coin a famous phrase, maybe not now or this year but next year and soon. And down the years when people read the transcript of the Prosecution case, they will see how little was there and they will be shocked that the case was allowed to continue. Before leading to some preliminaries and then the body of my submissions I need to address one spectre that hangs over this trial which is the spectre of moral equivalence which I addressed in my opening speech. And I simply reiterate everything I said there about why this case was brought. And I would now only say this, that if the Prosecution make a virtue tomorrow in their submissions of bringing this case because Naser Oric is a Muslim, then I say that brings shame on this Tribunal. Because to pursue Oric because he's a Muslim is to deny his individuality and to conduct an ethnically motivated Prosecution. It would be to turn this Tribunal into nothing better than an ethnic lynch mob and I'd say that it's judicial appeasement to indict a person to appease his erstwhile Serb enemy. Beyond that I won't address the falsity of the premise of moral equivalence except to point out this, that in every territory which the Serbs occupied they destroyed every mosque while the Bosnian Muslims, Croats, and Serbs loyal to the government left the churches alone, including in Srebrenica. But the greatest falsity is the presentation which the Prosecution has made in this case of the fighting forces in Srebrenica and of the ABiH as a Muslim army. You'll recall what General Sead Delic said on that subject only this Monday, that he was offended to be called a Muslim commander since his state, and army, were multi-ethnic, multi-denominational, unlike the ethnically based parastate Republika Srpska, and we have -- I should explain there is a PowerPoint presentation which we will be making and hard copies will be available of the slides afterwards and I thing -- believe we have the first slide to show. By way of explanation this is to facilitate presentation so that I don't need to read out full quotes or to provide references but that's the slide and you can see there what General Delic said, that he is personally offended when he is referred to as a Muslim or Bosniak commander. I would -- I won't dwell on this theme but Your Honours have repeatedly alluded to the importance of truth and reconciliation and broader issues at this Tribunal. I would simply say that if this -- amoral theory that all sides to the conflict must be prosecuted to show impartiality had been followed -- of -- after the Second World War, the resistance fighters of the Warsaw Ghetto uprising would have found themselves in the dock alongside Herman Goering and what message would have that sent to the post Holocaust world. Bad politics lies behind the decision to bring this case. But this case should be thrown out not because it's immoral or bad politics but because the evidence is simply not there. Now, I move on to preliminary remarks. In fact, if Your Honour's been following my skeleton that's by way of introduction. Just to set the parameters of my submission, today, this is obviously not a closing speech so we won't be addressing the case in its entirety by any means. And by the same token, no points are conceded on those points which we do not address, obviously. We know the Chamber has a duty to consider the case in its entirety in any event. The importance of the submission of no case to answer has been addressed by Your Honour on an earlier occasion so I won't dwell on that but it would be a huge waste of the Tribunal's resources to have months of trial which are unnecessary. We also we ask Your Honours and of course Your Honours are open minded as far as this application is concerned, but for it to mean anything, everyone of us should all be keeping in mind that as a possible result of this application, the application will succeed, the case will end here, and we will all go home. It cannot be considered a formality, just as the presumption of innocence is not something which we merely pay lip service to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: There is no application, Mr. Jones. As I said, this is not party driven any more. It's a responsibility that we have and it being a responsibility of the Trial Chamber to make sure that the accused is not put in a position where he has to answer things that are not proved on a prima facie basis broadly speaking within the standards for the -- recognised standards of Rule 98 bis. We will of course be going much more deeper than the two of you have because we have the responsibility. You have a responsibility towards your client. We have a responsibility towards your client too and towards justice.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, of course. I'm obliged, Your Honour. I'll avoid the word application and stick with submissions.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note could the booth please have copies of Mr. Jones's speech? We haven't got the document at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: There is no copy of his speech.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, I haven't written out the speech.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't think he is reading.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I have bullet pointed notes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What we can give you, I suppose, is the three-page notes or points.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Skeleton, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's what we have. Otherwise he didn't -- I didn't understand that he has a written speech.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: No. I have notes obviously but they are not of the nature which can be copied.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Again, I don't know how much help that's going to be to the interpreters because that's not what they meant.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I do trust though that if Your Honours consider that there is sufficient evidence or sufficient evidence on a particular charge or some point which needs to be elaborated, that you will of course give me the opportunity to address it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I would suggest that you address everything, Mr. Jones because don't expect us to tell you beforehand what our decision is going to be, particularly since we ourselves don't know what our decision is going to be. So --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It's in the spirit of not having to address the whole case, that it was merely to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But what I can assure you is that what you don't address, we will address. That's for sure. In other words, I, looking at these notes, for example, I notice that compared to plunder and wanton destruction et cetera, there is -- seems to be less when it comes to counts 1 and 2. It doesn't mean to say that in our exercise we will give to count 1 and 2 less importance than we will give -- it's up to you. It's more or less, in coming from the jurisdiction you come from, you should be in the position to know where your case is -- where the Prosecution case, let's put it like this, is strong, and where it is very weak or where it is extremely weak or non-existent. And --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, well, Your Honour it's particularly --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I mean, if you had a jury here and you were addressing the jury, yes, by all means, I would still hammer on, if I were you, even or where the Prosecution case is very strong, because you need to impress the jury. But with us, it doesn't work like that because we are capable, like you are, to figure out where the case of the Prosecution is very strong or where it is very weak or non-existent.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, it's simply this, that I am familiar in my jurisdiction with a situation where if a judge has a particular concern, if he doesn't particularly agree with one's submissions, then he will give one the opportunity to address that and in fact invite counsel to address a particular issue. And so it's really just to say that if there is some part of my submissions where Your Honours plainly do not agree or are not currently minded to agree, that you'll raise that with me and give me the opportunity to address any concerns. That was simply it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. Now, I would invite Your Honours also, now that the Prosecution case is closed, to go back to the opening speeches and to read them again now with a benefit of having heard all the evidence. In our submission you will see which of the parties really knew what the situation was in Srebrenica in 1992, 1993, and what the Prosecution case would establish. In the Prosecution opening speech, they made many exaggerated and overblown claims as to what their evidence would prove. To give one example, and a fairly basic one, going to the basic character of our client, in its opening speech the Prosecution sought to blacken Naser Oric's name and to show him as a swaggering warlord drunk with power. We put that characterisation to several witnesses and you'll recall that Dr. Mujkanovic rejected it, about as completely as one can, and if one sees the next slide, we see Dr. Mujkanovic's reaction, "No certainly not, there was no power to speak of in Srebrenica, to be anything in Srebrenica where you could hardly survive. It was a punishment rather than power." And that example in my submission is very telling because the Prosecution when it opened its case believed that its evident evidence would establish all sorts of things which it simply hasn't done. And for that reason, we say it's been misconceived from the start. Now, I'd like to turn to the elements of the offences very briefly. I'm certainly not going to it go through them in any length because it's set out in our pre-trial brief. The counts are set out in the indictment obviously, six counts, four crimes and two forms of liability. The crimes being murder, cruel treatment, wanton destruction, and plunder. And then the two forms of responsibility, obviously Article 7(1) instigating or aiding and abetting which is only applied to wanton destruction and to plunder and then Article 7(3) command responsibility. In our pre-trial brief we set out what we say the elements are and we can just briefly review that on PowerPoint. First we have the elements of plunder and I'm taking the charges in reverse order because I'll be first dealing with plunder and wanton destruction and then the detention charges even though that's in the reverse order of the indictment but I'm sure no confusion will be -- will be caused. So we have plunder, firstly, and as far as plunder is concerned, our submission firstly is that crimes charged as plunder are in fact none at all when one considers the defence of necessity which arises from the situation as it was in Srebrenica. Now, every legal system in the world recognises necessity created by circumstances as a defence to criminal charges, i.e. one is allowed to choose the lesser evil. In this case, theft over death by starvation. It's enshrined in Article 31(1)(D)(2) of the Rome Statute for ICC. It's also set out in the US model penal code, and we've also surveyed the jurisdictions of a dozen or so states and it's -- I think it can be safely said it's a customary provision. In Germany one has the concepts of Notstand I believe it is, necessity caused by circumstances. And Malta is also one of the jurisdictions we surveyed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think we can agree that you don't need to dwell on this much longer because necessity is one of the basic principles of criminal law in the area of criminal responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's recognised worldwide.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: We also says say that it's uncontested that the Prosecution evidence has established over and again that there were thousands of civilians literally starving to death in Srebrenica and that they went out on these actions to get food. One witness put the necessity of stealing food very simply, it's the slide 2.1.1 Mensud Omerovic, "We could either die, starve to death or we could get killed trying to get food, otherwise we would die anyway so we had to go in search of food." That was the situation of thousands of civilians in Srebrenica. The Prosecution bears the burdens of proof in this case so let them prove that these civilians did not need to steal food to survive, that there was some alternative open to them. We say that any developed legal system has to allow this Defence in light of what Your Honour has said I will pass briefly over the next slide but mountain climbers lost in a storm may take refuge in a house or may appropriate provisions. A developed legal system must have better ways of dealing with such problems than to refer only to the letter, particularly prohibitions. Turning now to wanton destruction, and I'll come back to these -- I'll come back to each of the charges in relation to the evidence. At the moment I'm just dealing with the elements of the crimes and where we say that even the crimes themselves have not been shown. Then we move on obviously to questions of Article 7(3) liability and Article 7(1) liability. Wanton destruction must be large scale and not justified by military necessity. The Prosecution has not shown in reach of these actions, and when I say "not shown," I mean, obviously, to the standards of proof required at this stage, that there has been large-scale destruction. There has been no attempt at any sort of inventory to say what was destroyed wantonly as opposed to what was destroyed during combat operations, and by whom it was done. The OTP has to positively show the absence of military necessity. It's an element of the offence rather than it being for the Defence to show the presence of military necessity. Now it can be necessary to destroy buildings which the enemy are using to fire from, and it can be necessary to destroy property to deny the enemy ground. That's recognised in the jurisprudence relating to this crime. Now, I would just refer and I did alert my learned friends to a couple of authorities which I would mention very briefly, but in the list, Hostages Trial case before the US military Tribunal at Nuremberg in 1948, it was stated quote, "Military necessity permits a belligerent, subject to the laws of war, to apply any amount and kind of force to compel the complete submission of the enemy with the least possible expenditure of time, life, and money." In general, it sanctions measures by an occupant necessary to protect the safety of his forces and to facilitate the success of his operations. It is lawful to destroy railways, lines of communication, or any other property that might be utilised by the enemy. Private homes and churches may even be destroyed if necessary for military operations." And in the Von Leeb High Command Trial case before the US military Tribunal at Nuremberg in 1948, the Tribunal writing of the arduous conditions of the defendants, where their commands were in serious danger of being cut off, said "what constitutes devastation beyond military necessity in these situations requires detailed proof of an operational and tactical nature". I should add most of these defendants, if not all, were acquitted even of scorched earth policies. Now the Prosecution dropped their military expert and so Your Honours have not been presented with any proof of an operational and tactical nature. Instead, and this is the Prosecution's approach in this case, they will invite you to assume, to guess, that any damage to property was unlawful. Just as they would invite you - and I'll come to this later - but to assume that whenever someone died in prison, it was murder. Leaps -- you will be required to make leaps of faith in order to keep -- keep this case on its weary feet. As far as that assumption or that invitation to infer that any damage must have been caused unlawfully, that simply does not have any bearing on military reality. Now, murder, and that's slide 2.3, again is not simply a matter of assuming that any death in custody must be a murder. There are detailed provisions of actus reus, mens rea. Actus reus, a death caused by subordinates of the accused, for a command responsibility case, and mens rea, that those causing death possessed the requisite intent. Now the Prosecution has not shown that the deaths charged in the indictment were all murders and as I say it's not every death that is a murder, nor every battery which results in death a murder. There are varying degrees of homicides, involuntary and voluntary manslaughter. Now, I would ask Your Honours to think of our own national system. Murder is not charged lightly and people aren't convicted lightly of murder. Detailed lengthy trials take place to examine the minutiae of whether or not a particular killing is a murder. But as I say the Prosecution has not attempted to prove that identified perpetrators acted with the requisite murderous intent, that they substantially caused the death of the victims, much less that those people were the -- were specifically -- those specific people were subordinates of Naser Oric and the other elements. Cruel treatment which is on slide P2.4, the elements are set out there, and, of course, the evidence shown that there were people who were mistreated, badly mistreated in Srebrenica, but we say not by subordinates of Naser Oric and we will come to that when we address Article 7(3). The elements of Article 7(1) liability are on our slide 2.5. And then command responsibility 7.3, that's P2.6. And these are three cumulative requirements which can be summarised as subordinates committing the crimes, knowledge or information that the crimes have been committed by the subordinates and failure to take necessary measures. And again I would ask Your Honours to be robust. In a national system one would not brush over these requirements. They are cumulative and if there is not sufficient evidence of any of those three elements, then the case has to be stopped at half time. Now, the evidence with regard to the third element of measures, the failure to take measures to prevent or punish the crimes, the evidence as far as that has been concerned has been of a lack of any proper structure in Srebrenica at the relevant time, no judges, prosecutors, military police, et cetera. That element we will address in closing speech if we get there. It's not something I propose to address in these submissions; I'll be concentrating on the first two elements. But we would just illustrate the impossibility of prevention of plunder and wanton destruction with reference to the evidence of Dr. Nedret Mujkanovic describing what he termed the sociological phenomenon of thousands of starving, desperate, terrified civilians who were out of control. That's slide number 3, and I'll give Your Honours a moment to read that. It describes the absence of any means for Srebrenica to function and then on the next slide, yes, describes it as "a phenomenon that nobody who hasn't experienced it can understand. Sometimes civilians would enter these villages even before the troops and sometimes many of them were wounded, many of them were killed, they didn't get hold of the food although it was food they came in for in the first place." That phenomenon of thousands of so-called Torbari streaming into villages before, during, and after actions, has been plainly attested to by Prosecution witnesses so much that it must be beyond dispute. Even Serb witnesses, for example Slavoljub Zikic described the scene in Fakovici on the 4th of October 1992 thus: "I think a civilised nation may find it difficult to understand what I'm telling you. It was seething from all sides," and he goes on. And he accepted, Mr. Zikic, that no army could stop these civilians from getting food. The same phenomenon was described in relation to all the raids. You'll recall it's merely by way of another example how Mensud Omerovic described the scene in Bjelovac on the 14th of December 1992, and that's slide 5. When asked about lines kilometres long, he said "it was a long, uninterrupted column of the elderly, women, children, as young as ten, and it was already December," and he accepted that these were desperate people ready to kill for food, ready to kill each other for food. And Dr. Mujkanovic also saw the seen in Bjelovac and described it as "rivers of people, 2.000 people, pushing towards those villages. It was impossible to describe the scene." . Indeed, we would submit that at this stage the close of the Prosecution case, that their case on plunder and wanton destruction was nullified was absolutely nullified by the up challenged and uncontradicted evidence of their own witness, Dr. Mujkanovic, that no one could stop the civilians and that Oric didn't aid or abet the plunder. And that's the next slide, 6.1. This is a Prosecution witness an insider, to whom I put the key questions of this trial: "Do you think Naser Oric could have prevented civilians from stealing those things during military actions?" "Not only Naser Oric, nobody, nobody, could look after these people. These people were left to their own means. Everybody was left to look after themselves." "So may I take it that the answer is, no, he couldn't prevent that from happening." "I said that there wasn't and could not have been any authority or organisation, be it the War Presidency or an individual who could have done that." "Would the same apply for the destruction of Serb property?" "There was no mechanism, no instrument that could have prevented that from happening." How can the Prosecution continue with this case on plunder and wanton destruction when their own witnesses in unchallenged and uncontradicted evidence have told you that? If Your Honours recognise that reality, that neither Oric nor anyone could prevent these crimes, you're not being soft or letting Oric off the hook. You're simply being realistic and humane. Now, that is by way of background. I'd like to deal with the charges in more detail, starting, as I say, with Article 7(1) and charges of plunder and looting. And for that, as I said by way of introduction, the charges brought under Article 7(1), there is quite simply no evidence whatsoever - and I emphasise that, no evidence whatsoever - that Oric instigated or aided and abetted people to loot and burn. On the contrary, only evidence is that he saw it as a problem and wanted to stop it. If we see slide 6.2 and Dr. Mujkanovic, and "What was the opinion of Naser Oric in that regard?" And this was obviously in relation to these offences if they are such. "He had the same opinion, he was against people burning houses but there was simply nothing that he could do. He did not have a way of stopping them. It's not that he simply didn't approve, he fiercely opposed this." Again, how can the Prosecution seriously continue with charges under Article 7(1) that Oric aided and abetted and instigated offences when their own witness who testified for several days, who was an insider, worked in the hospital, spoke to many, many people, gives that sort of evidence? He also spoke, Dr. Mujkanovic of the distances between hamlets and villages in this area. And thousands of people and the impossibility of preventing damage to property. And again this is where the context is even more important, the context of Srebrenica in 1992, 1993, even if this were not enough. Remember, the population of Srebrenica was faced with an impending massacres by the Serbs in this period, and that -- that's not simply my assertion, that's been the evidence of many insiders, that people feared that they would die, it wasn't a question of when but a -- a question of if but when, and is the suggestion really that the fighting forces of Srebrenica should have deployed every able-bodied man to join arms and stand around these villages like some sort of riot police to guard Serb property night and day? As our client said in interview, "What idiot would do that when he would probably end up just getting shot from behind by some civilian who wanted to get through? Not only that but the result would no doubt have been that the enclave would have fallen in 1992 instead of 1995." I turn now to Article 7(3) in relation to plunder and wanton destruction. And as I've said there are the three elements and so no question but that the Prosecution has to prove all three elements beyond a reasonable doubt and at this stage satisfy Your Honours that there is sufficient evidence to sustain a conviction. And as I said we will address the question of subordinates firstly because we say we don't even get on to the other elements. Now, in all the eight months of this trial, with evidence being brought three hours and 45 minutes every day of those eight months, there has not been evidence that a single crime was committed by a single subordinate of Oric. For plunder, the clear evidence has been that it was committed civilians. And if the Prosecution is going to argue that an old woman stealing a chicken is a subordinate of Naser Oric, then the law of command responsibility has broken all bounds of sense and entered the realm of the absurd. In fact, there is already a backlash against the extended notion of command responsibility as it's been applied by this Tribunal. It is an exceptional form of liability, command responsibility, and as such it has to be construed narrowly and strictly. Mainly we say, women and children and civilian men are not Oric's subordinates. Plainly he had no effective control over these people. And they were the ones when were going to get food on their own initiative. You will recall the evidence of Mensud Omerovic, slide number 7, "Each person on their own went trying to get some food for themselves and families, entire families went, including women and children." "So the armed forces did not organise you to join them in their actions, operations." "No, absolutely no." Again, Prosecution witness uncontradicted evidence. And Hakija Meholjic, Dr. Nedret Mujkanovic, and all the others who actually lived in Srebrenica and who actually now the situation there said the same thing. For the Serb witnesses in the villages where the actions took place, for the most part, overwhelmingly, they know they were attacked, but for the most part, and I'm willing to discuss exceptions, the attackers are unidentified persons who cannot even competently be described as soldiers never mind as subordinates of Naser Oric. So it's the insiders, i.e., people who were in Srebrenica, who were the persons who have been turned to for reliable information. Indeed in any case based on command responsibility, that's the only way that a case can be made out. And the insiders, every one of them in our submission, have failed to confirm the most basic thesis of the Prosecution. Judge Mensud Omerovic, Dr. Mujkanovic, Hakija Meholjic, Becir Bogilovic, Ibrahim Becirovic, none of them have confirmed that any crimes were committed by Oric's subordinates. And that in itself is incredibly striking. Anyone in a position of power has enemies. Those envious of his position, and even more so in war, and even more so when a 25 year old has any authority. And if I may digress on this theme, wartime leaders, Winston Churchill, Franklin Roosevelt, had fierce opponents. And it would always be possible for some hate figure to crawl out from under a stone and to point an accusing finger. But here you don't have a single insider pointing an accusing finger at Naser Oric. So the only way you can get at Article 7(3) liability for Naser Oric is with a fundamentalist hypothesis that every man, woman, and child, every displaced person, every refugee, out of tens of thousands of people, every displaced person with a gun who was chased by the Serbs into Srebrenica and wandered about unregistered and unknown, that he was a subordinate of Naser Oric. And that Oric, God-like almost, knew of what every one of these people were doing at any given moment. You would have to posit a thesis that absurd to get close to Article 7(3) liability. And that absurd, fundamentalist hypothesis is in any event contradicted by the Prosecution's own evidence that many fighters even were not under Oric's control. And so it would be a shame to go anywhere near such a crude and false theory. If I can approach this issue -- approach the issue this way in order to make it clear. Firstly you'll find this on point 6 of my skeleton. Sorry, if I can locate my skeleton. First of all one has to distinguish between attackers and looters and burners. These are different issues, attackers can behave properly as fighters while others exploit the situation to come in and to loot and to burn. And indeed time and again that has been the consistent evidence given by witnesses. So for that reason one can't conflate and run together the issue of who the attackers were and who the people looting and burning were because there is no necessary identity at all between the two of them. In fact it's intellectually lazy to do so but more importantly it would lead to downright injustice, because all the evidence is that civilians would go in both before, during and after actions. As far as fighters are concerned, it's not a crime to conduct raids to get ammunition and arms when the fighters desperately need those things and when they are under siege. And the allowance to take war booty is part of customary international law. And there is authority for that but again it's probably not contested but in the ICRC's very recent publication on customary international humanitarian law - it's published by Cambridge University Press this year - rules of international humanitarian law, customary rules are set out. Rule 49 is on war booty and it says this. "The parties to the conflict may seize military equipment belonging to the adverse party as war booty." And that provision exists in every military manual in the world. So again if the Prosecution is going to suggest that Srebrenica's fighters committed theft when they took arms and ammunition from the enemy, the enemy that's killing them, then I say they've lost all contact with reality. And we have evidence that war booty was seized in every action. So the Prosecution seeking to show, and they haven't succeeded even on the most basic test, but to show that Oric commanded some of these actions doesn't even begin to establish their case. They have to show that in those actions, even if they were commanded by Naser Oric, which we deny, that the looting and destruction was done by his subordinates. And without military necessity and that he knew that his subordinates committed the crimes and so on. The Prosecution may invite you to consider that anyone wearing any part of the military uniform is not only a soldier but a soldier in a unit commanded by Oric. Again, a huge leap of faith which I trust Your Honours will not make because there is no proof, there has been no proof of that. The evidence has been that in 1992 and 1993, being in a uniform or not says absolutely nothing about whether the person is a fighter or not, never mind as to which units they are in. And again referring to my skeleton, the first point, A, referring to the fundamental disorganisation of Srebrenica's fighting forces in 1992, and 1993, again, all the evidence of the insiders has come together on that point that the armed forces in Srebrenica were improvised and completely disorganised in 1992, 1993, without uniforms for the most part, without barracks, without weapons, without salaries, without ranks, without badges, without insignia, without anything which one would expect of an army. Quite simply, it was not an army; it was a resistance against the Serb occupation. Now the Serbs in the villages from whom we've heard who have consistently emphasised that they were in their villages the whole time and little aware of what was going on around them, were not in a position to know how the forces in Srebrenica were organised because they were on the other side of the enemy lines and that's emerged clearly from their testimony. Now, because whether or not someone wore a uniform is no guide to whether they are a fighter or not, for that reason it's impossible for any of these Serb witnesses to say by sight whether someone was a soldier or not or whether he was in a unit and therefore they are not in a position, any of them, to say that these people were subordinates of Naser Oric. Unless, of course, they could say I identified so and so at the scene and then there is evidence that so and so was a subordinate of Naser Oric. And that's the sort of evidence which you would expect in a trial of this nature it's the sort of evidence which Your Honours would be entitled to expect, that there is actually some link between these people on the ground and Naser Oric. But again, there isn't. And you'll find in all the other cases in this Tribunal, you'll find that chain of a crime committed by someone, an identifiable perpetrator, that perpetrator being placed in a unit under command of the accused, the accused then being informed specifically that his subordinate who committed a crime and then that he had done nothing. That's a real case based on command responsibility. You have none of that here. As far as documentary evidence is concerned on this matter, in my submission, in our submission, an Article 7(3) case depends on insiders. It cannot turn on documents which no witnesses accepted as accurate documents purportedly setting out the structure of the armed forces.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Wouldn't that be an argument for the final stages of the trial, if the trial goes on?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I merely wanted to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: At the present moment, for the purposes of Rule 98 bis, if a document is such that for obvious reasons cannot be thrown out completely, then it has to be accepted for what it shows on the face of it. Irrespective of how much credibility we will give it in due course but what I mean to say is this: If there is a document, however much you disagree with it, which we cannot throw a priori because of obvious reasons, which says there was such and such an attack on such and such a day by such and such units under the command of Naser Oric, it's there. Now, whether that is correct or not, whether it really happened, how much weight you give to the document, whether it's been forged or whether it's genuine these --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: That's entirely clear, Your Honour. As far as -- I won't go into a discussion of specific documents in any detail but of course that depends on what the witness has said about the document and, for example, if a document purports to say that forces were in the Srebrenica TO, and then General Delic says, well, in fact, it doesn't mean at the time they were in that formation, that's his evidence, and that's the Prosecution's evidence. And that in my submission, does have to be taken into account.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Certainly. What I meant to say is this: That if there is a document, Mr. Jones, that says what I just said, I mean, which is just -- I'm just inventing it, and even if there are 40 witnesses that have come here and testified that Mr. Oric had absolutely nothing to do with that operation, or that action, call it whatever you like, still we have the document for the purpose of the Rule 98 bis we cannot exclude it and we cannot weigh one against the other. This is the --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I take it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I know that you know this. It's not a question of trying to explain to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, taking the Prosecution at its highest, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Sorry to have interrupted you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Not at all, Your Honour. I was going to move to another slide which is on the -- the issue of the forces in Srebrenica being organised on a voluntary basis. It was the evidence of Dr. Mujkanovic but indeed it was the evidence of Judge Omerovic, Becir Bogilovic, all the insiders. It was left up to people to decide whether or not to be a fighter. That since no one could actually provide them with a gun or with food, that it was simply up to people whether or not to participate. The result of that, in fact, I would also just go on to slide 9 which was Dr. -- sorry, Judge Mensud Omerovic on the same theme. "People who were armed, the combatants, did not live in barracks. They lived with their families; precisely so, they lived with their wives and children. They would stand guard to everyone knew when the next operation would be," et cetera. The consequence of this in terms of Article 7(3) is vitally important. Because unless you actually know someone's identity, you cannot tell from their appearance whether they are a fighter or a civilian and I trust that that's clear. In terms of the characterisation of these fighting forces, Colonel Tucker when I put to him the earlier quote from Dr. Mujkanovic agreed that the fighting force in Srebrenica was a levee en masse, which has a feature of not being formed into armed units, not being formed into units means not having a single commander, and to be organised in the hierarchical fashion, which is a precondition for Article 7(3) to apply, and without going into detailed legal argument, levee en masse, I would simply say or referred to in the Lieber Instructions, the Brussels Conference of 1874, Oxford manual, Hague regulations, and the Geneva Conventions. It's a well-known concept in international humanitarian law. So in our submission, Article 7(3) and it's a legal submission, cannot apply to a levee en masse for this very reason. It lacks the feature of a command structure in which you can even speak of superiors and subordinates, and we is see in slide 10.1, Colonel Tucker, an experienced military officer and recipient of the military cross agreeing that as far as he could tell, Srebrenica's fighters were levee en masse. And then elaborating on what he said at some point about reports of some people being forced to fight, he said, it's slide 10.2, "the vast majority of people were volunteers. Only a very small number are being forced to fight." And this was agreed to by Hakija Meholjic, Mensud Omerovic, Becir Bogilovic. Now this lack of organisation obviously goes to a number of issues, effective control, knowledge, means to prevent or punish, but we are approaching it now in the context of it being impossible to say on the basis of mere appearance who is a fighter, who is a civilian, and if someone is a fighter, what unit they are in. And just on that theme, we have another slide, I'll go through it very quickly, 11.1, Hakija Meholjic, "It is not an organised army, it was not a real army, and I can claim that before God and the whole world that this army was not organised." Then he went on also to say "there was no bread, let alone ranks, there were no patches," the next slide, "no markings, by which the troops could be distinguished from civilians." That brings us to the issue of ribbons which is an a matter which I would like to address. Before that, it may just be to make the point, which has just been made more clearly, but we see the slide there at 12.1, Ibrahim Becirovic who repeatedly referred to poorly organised units throughout his testimony. He said at the time, "I didn't even think that there were persons who could be referred to as commanders. In my view those were still poorly organised groups." And he also went to say that nothing operated in a coordinated manner. That's slide 12.2. "Nobody had an obligation to go and help, this was not an organised structure that could coordinate the activities of groups which existed in local communities." That's absence of even an ability to coordinate never mind effectively to control. Now turning to the next heading in my skeleton, fighters not soldiers, again it's perhaps a recapitulation on the same theme but all of the insiders and I would count Colonel Tucker as an insider because he spent time in Srebrenica agreed that one could only talk about fighters and poorly organised groups around -- organised around men, Hakija's men, Zulfo's men, Akif's men, Ejub's men, rather than an army with soldiers. So that when Serb witnesses spoke of seeing soldiers there was no consistent usage whether it meant a young man with a rifle or someone wearing a bit of uniform, and they certainly were not able to say whether any of these people belonged to any unit. We see that also on PowerPoint slide 13 and 14 as well. I won't dwell because I think the point is clear. Colonel Tucker there saying that "the definition of soldier as is understood in a democratic country, in Bosnia is not particularly relevant." In fact I would like to skip forward over C of my skeleton, that's 7(C) which I think I've already probably dealt with in sufficient detail, the lack of reliable information on the Serb side regarding of the organisation of fighting men in Srebrenica. The reality is and I'll just take it very shortly, as I've said that Serbs in the surrounding villages could not possibly know whether the people they saw in actions were fighters or not. Some of them did claim to have some idea but by way of a couple of examples, Slavisa Eric based the notion that Naser Oric had commanded the attack on Jezestica on the fact -- well, on what he later said was no reliable information whatsoever, "no valid data," were his words. Nikola Popovic based his conclusion, if one can call it that, that Naser Oric was involved in the action in Kravica on the fact that when he came back months later there was graffiti which said Naser Oric. In my submission that shows what passed for information amongst the Serbs in these towns and villages was utterly unreliable and that the only credible testimony is that for example given by C007, PowerPoint slide 17.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Again, please, Mr. Jones, again, I need to remind you, that for the purpose of rule 98, we are not interested in what is credible and what is not credible.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So when you put it to us what's credible is the evidence of C007, but what Nikola Popovic said or what the other guy said, that's not credible, that's not the argument that we want to hear today.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, I'm aware of that Your Honour and perhaps it was an unfortunate choice of word. Of course, at the same time, I would submit that if, for example, Nikola Popovic says Naser Oric commanded an attack on Kravica. I know because I saw graffiti three months later which said Naser Oric. That is a case where Your Honours can say that is not -- even taken at its highest, it doesn't take us anywhere.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Definitely, but then don't try to draw comparisons.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: No, okay. Indeed. I would just draw attention to what C007 said there, "Would it be right to say that for you a soldier is basically a Muslim fighter whether or not he belongs to an army. How should I know that a person is a member of an army or not? It's not something that I can tell." And that, I think, is reflected in the evidence this that was given by 99 per cent of the Serb witnesses, in fact they really had no idea who had attacked them. Now I come to my next point which again I can perhaps take shortly if it's a matter which Your Honours concede but the evidence has been that there were many groups of fighters or units which were not under the command of Naser Oric. The Prosecution's own evidence has clearly shown that, for example, well, firstly, that Hakija's men, Hakija Meholjic's men were clearly both de jure and de facto not under Naser Oric. And that Zulfo's men and Akif's men, Zulfo Tursunovic and Akif Ustic's men were de facto not under the control of Naser Oric. And that there were many other locally organised groups of fighters who were not under Oric. And the consequence of this is terribly important because even if in a given action one were to say, well, this able-bodied person with a rifle is possibly a fighter, even if one could make that leap, it's for the Prosecution to satisfy that you perpetrators of crimes were subordinates of Naser Oric, and how do they say that you can be satisfied that that wasn't one of Hakija's men or one of Zulfo's men or one of Akif's men or one of the men of all these other units which were in the Srebrenica area operating at that time? They can't simply invite to you skip over that and to just assume the very worst for our client, that anyone who remotely resembled a fighter was a subordinate of Oric. The independence of Hakija Meholjic and his men was the uncontradicted evidence, evidence of Hakija Meholjic himself, of Nedret Mujkanovic, of Becir Bogilovic, and I believe everyone who testified on this matter. We can see a couple of slides just by way of example on that. Slide 18, and he was asked, "Would you agree that Hakija and his unit, that Hakija was an independent commander, that is independent of Naser Oric?" "Yes, I would agree." "And Hakija didn't report to Naser, did he?" "No, he didn't." "And neither did Hakija's men then, they were neither under Oric's command and control." "No, they weren't." And that amounts to tens if not hundreds of men in Srebrenica, in fact the units as we saw from Exhibit D299 was actually called the Srebrenica unit, who were independent of Naser Oric's command. We can see actually, or we did see that with Exhibit D299 and General Sead Delic, the next slide, 19, agreeing that according to that document, the Srebrenica unit under Hakija Meholjic was not with any formation, including the Srebrenica TO. He confirmed that that was correct. Hakija Meholjic himself was crystal clear about never being under Naser Oric's command and that's slide number 20. He did not accept Naser as commander. He did not -- Oric did not issue orders to Hakija Meholjic and he did not reports to Oric. Very clear, uncontroverted testimony. Becir Bogilovic, too, said how throughout this time Hakija waged a policy of his own. Looking at the time, I suppose we do have until 10.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Take your time. Even if -- I don't know how much more time you need. You can have the entire sitting, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I think I'll finish this heading of the independence of various units and then that would be a good it time to take a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Certainly. What I mean to say, if you want to go a little bit beyond the 10.30, I don't think anyone is going to question that. We will stop when it's convenient for you and then we will resume, we will have the break -- provided we don't go beyond two hours. All right?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. Overall my submissions may be longer than two hours but I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Choose yourself the best time for you to have a break.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I move to the independence of Akif Ustic and his men, and again Dr. Mujkanovic said that Naser Oric had no control of Akif's unit, that's on slide number 20, those were units beyond his control. That was confirmed by Hakija Meholjic, we see that on slide 21, that Akif Ustic went into action on his own initiative and, according to his opinion, without Naser's knowledge. And Becir Bogilovic also confirmed that Akif Ustic also had an independent command. We don't have slide, but that was from the 22nd of March 2005. There is no need obviously to take Your Honours through all that evidence. You've -- you're aware of it and you've heard it. And then we have evidence that Zulfo Tursunovic and his unit were not under the affective control of Naser Oric and that he ran his area of Sutjeska without even allowing Naser Oric in without his permission. That's slide number 22. Is it possible that Zulfo Tursunovic in fact acted as an independent commander, at least in certain matters or certain actions? In most of the cases, he ran an entire area and he wouldn't let anyone interfere with his job. He ran the Sutjeska area and he wouldn't allow anyone near. You couldn't go there unless you'd been invited there specifically by him. That was the only way you could go. Now, if Naser Oric wasn't even allowed into the area commanded by Zulfo Tursunovic, it can hardly be said that he had effective control over Zulfo Tursunovic and that Zulfo Tursunovic was his subordinate. And again Becir Bogilovic confirmed the independence Zulfo Tursunovic, and that he had an independent command, as he called it, in the area of Sutjeska. This means there were large groups of men in the town of Srebrenica and Sutjeska over whom Naser Oric did not have control. So if Hakija's men or Akif's men or Zulfo's men committed crimes it's quite simply not command responsibility it's not Article 7(3) liability, because they are not Naser Oric's subordinates. And as I say you cannot simply draw the conclusion least favourable to the accused, that anyone committing a crime is his subordinate. Finally, there are -- there was ample evidence of other independent units in the immediate Srebrenica area. There was uncontradicted evidence of Ibro Becirovic that a Becir Mekanic and Fadil Turkovic had groups of armed men operating in the Sutjeska area who clashed with Serbs, so who were engaged in combat actions against the Serbs during this time and in this place. Becir Bogilovic also confirmed that these units, he was referring I believe to Becir Mekanic's unit, never entered the composition of the armed forces of Srebrenica. And indeed it goes on and on. Ahmo Tihic and his unit from Skelani acted autonomously from Oric. That was the evidence of Dr. Mujkanovic and others. It's slide number 23. Sorry, slide 23 deals with the independence of units even aside from these named units which I've mentioned of Hakija, Akif, et cetera, that there were a lot of local commanders who had autonomy. He said "these men trusted their leaders and that's how they became commanders. They were not appointed. They were self-appointed commanders who were approved by the fighters who lived in certain localities, in certain villages or in certain parts of the area. If the men didn't want to do something, then they didn't do it." So in this situation, Your Honours, just to summarise on the above, we already have evidence of thousands of civilians going to Serb villages for food, not under Naser Oric's control, a situation incidentally created by the Serbs by keeping the place under siege. We have displaced persons with weapons and bits of old uniforms from their military service, drifting into the Srebrenica area without anyone even knowing who they are, never mind controlling them. Those people were also going in search of food and clashing with Serbs. We have significant -- well, poorly organised units but units nonetheless which were not under Oric's control, Hakija's, Akif's Zulfo's, Ahmo Tihic's, Becir Mekanic's. Plus in all of this we have local villages simply spontaneously resisting the Serb advance. Now in all this morass, are Your Honours really going to say that there was sufficient evidence for the unsupported, unjustified and least favourable conclusion for the accused, namely that any given person seen committing a crime is a subordinate of Oric without any hard proof to that effect? And I would really insist on that, and on Your Honours putting the Prosecution to the test on this. How on earth can they be satisfied and how can they satisfied you with this mass of armed and untamed humanity that a single act of plunder or destruction has been done by one of Naser Oric's subordinates? They can't be satisfied and you can't be satisfied. Your Honours, I'll take the break there, if that's appropriate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Certainly, Mr. Jones. I think we can have a 30-minute break. You will have a well-deserved rest. Is that enough, 30 minutes?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Perfectly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Are you ready to continue, Mr. Jones o are you like some more time?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: No, no, no, that's fine, Your Honour. In fact my -- my initial estimate was that it would be around two hours and I think I manage to be around it will be around two, two and a half hours. I certainly won't go to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Just take -- take as much -- you have got the whole day for you, I mean it's --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, yes, thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- even if you need to stay beyond quarter to 2.00, we'll stay.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: That's very kind. During the break, however, I've had another look at my skeleton and seen that certain points don't need recapitulation and so at this stage I'm actually at point 7 H, the meaninglessness of uniforms as designating fighters in organised units. And I'll just say a couple of points on that and then move on. And in fact, I think -- I think I will keep my headphones on, actually, so I can hear myself. Good. Yes, there are certain points in the skeleton which I won't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Hearing yourself is a good thing, a good thing. Make sure that you don't start arguing with yourself.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: That would be a very worrying sign. For some reason it helps to have my voice -- yes. Now, Your Honour, there are points which I think I've developed sufficiently this morning. As far as uniforms are concerned, I really just wanted to summarise by saying that the evidence brought by the Prosecution establishes two things clearly, that one can be a fighter not in any sort of uniform and secondly one can be in a uniform or a bit of uniform and not be a fighter. I won't dwell greatly on those -- those areas because you will have the PowerPoint slides where we have extracts of quotations on that theme and because it's in the skeleton. I would just briefly go to slide 26 which is Mr. Okanovic, a Serb witness, who confirmed there that a uniform meant nothing, and that someone could be wearing a uniform or a piece of uniform and not be a soldier but simply possess it from military service and he agreed -- and he agreed that people would wear uniform simply because it was warm and well made and not because they were in any unit. And the other slides on this theme are Colonel Tucker and it's slides 24 and 25. We don't need to go through them I just say it for the record, and Dr. Mujkanovic, slides 27 and 28, saying that as Dr. Mujkanovic summarised it to speak about uniforms in Srebrenica is a futile exercise. And of course I make that point to say that in any of these actions saying that someone was in uniform and drawing inferences based on that is meaningless. I do want to dwell a little on ribbons, the question of ribbons and bands, and that's on -- in the skeleton, it's point 7 H and then the bullet point which is entitled "absence of ribbon or identifying feature in an action means that the persons were positively not an organised unit." I can develop that a little, then I'll move on to detention charges. Now, Hakija Meholjic, General Sead Delic, and others said that the only way to distinguish fighters from others in actions was by the use of ribbons. Indeed, Hakija Meholjic said there were no other distinguishing features among fighters. So, in fact, one can say, and it's the Prosecution's own evidence on this subject from its own witnesses, that persons not wearing ribbons in an action must be presumed not to be fighters. If we see slide number 30, it's General Sead Delic, I'll just read from that. Being shown Prosecution Exhibits, he said "All of those who were in battlefield and took part in combat did not have the bands, either around the head or around the arm were considered to be enemy soldiers and as such were targeted." And then when he commented on P89 relating to Bjelovac, I asked him, "So according to this, and according to what you said if you weren't wearing a yellow ribbon in Bjelovac, you weren't a participant in the action." And he answered, "It would mean that you didn't belong to that part of the armed formations; hence, you were an enemy, and as such a legitimate target." The point of ribbons is that that shows that the fighters themselves could not distinguish between fighters and civilians based merely on the clothes that they were wearing. And that is the final demonstration, if you'd like, that wearing uniform is not a guide to whether someone was a fighter or not. That's why ribbons were needed. So in our submission, for a case to go forward on any of the charges regarding actions in Serb towns and villages you would need someone as an identifiable fighter, that is someone actually wearing a ribbon or a band committing one of those offences and then there would need to be a demonstration that that person was a subordinate of Naser Oric rather than a subordinate of any of these other formations which we've heard about. And as we say the evidence does not get anywhere close, and that's why we say those charges should all be dismissed. I'd like to move on to the detention charges. And as -- as -- by way of general introduction on the detention matters, it's clear that people were badly beaten in Srebrenica in the prison. We don't deny that, and we say it's tragic and terribly wrong that it ever happened and we have every sympathy for those who suffered and for the families of those who died. But we only say that these crimes are not attributable in any way to Naser Oric. He was a fighter on the line. He was not a civilian police chief or a prison governor in any sense of the word and that the Prosecution evidence does not make out a sufficient case that he was anything of that description. He is not responsible for anyone's murder or for anyone's cruel treatment. Starting with murder, murder as I've said this morning and as I'm sure we'll all agree, is the most serious crime that exists in domestic criminal systems, and accordingly domestic systems do not lightly convict persons of that crime, nor in systems which know of the institution of a no-case-to-answer submission, a case is permitted to go to the jury unless all the elements have been made out at least to a prima facie standard. Not every death is the result of a murder, nor is every beating which leads to the death of the victim a murder. There are many forms of homicide which are not murder. Now, at the ICTY, as a general rule in Article 7(3) cases where murder is charged, you'll at least have the commander being informed of killings, of murders, of massacres. You'll have, for example, a member of the international community informing a commander of a possible massacre here -- here or a massacre there. Or you'll have a subordinate informing his superior that there might have been killings. And normally, in fact, it's of terrible massacres, as for example happened in Srebrenica in 1995, July 1995. In Yamashita, the case which gave rise to the law of command responsibility, the figures of murdered civilians were staggering. There was 5.000 people in Batangas, 7.800 people in Laguna, 8.000 civilians killed in Manila, as well as many other massacres. And then, it's to be seen whether or not the commander looked into these reports of massacres. But here the Prosecution has charged Naser Oric with 7 murders and there is not one jot of evidence, that is to say not one line of testimony or one exhibit which says that anyone ever informed Oric of these murders. Not even that he was informed of killings possibly by his subordinates and that he was put on notice to investigate, there's no proof that he was informed that any of these people had been unlawfully killed, only that Kukic, Dragutin Kukic, had died, and he was told, if it was Naser Oric, someone allegedly being Naser Oric, that he died of a heart attack. The fact is people do die of heart attacks and as a matter of law, it cannot be said that someone dying of a heart attack in a prison puts one on notice of a suspicious death. Obviously if there were two or three or four heart attacks, that's one thing, but this is Srebrenica, 1992, when people were dying of all sorts of ailments every day. And that's one of the murders. One about the other six? Will Your Honours really allow this case to continue with our client being charged with six murders when he was never even informed that these persons died? And just parenthetically, there was a -- an extract from the interview with our client which was played referring to Mirzet being involved in the killing. Mirzet Halilovic, as we've heard, was removed from his post and died in January 1993, but that's not that -- that matter is not one of the -- let me rephrase that. There has been no evidence that any of these killings were attributable to Mirzet. Now we set out the elements of murder in the pre-trial brief, and there are specific actus reus and mens rea requirements. Indeed there is authority from the ICTY and ICTR that premeditation is required for murder, and I would refer to the Trial Chamber ruling in the Kupreskic Trial Judgement at paragraphs 560 to 561. Apology, I don't have the date of that Trial Judgement. But in that judgement they noted that -- in Kayishema it was noted that "The standard of mens rea required is intentional and premeditated killing. The result is pre-meditated when the actor formulated his intent to kill after a cool moment of reflection." Now, we are not insisting. It's a matter for Your Honours, really, as the guardians of the law as to whether premeditation is required or not. But certainly murder as is commonly understood requires a very high intentional element. The fact is in this case we haven't had evidence of what the mens rea of the perpetrators was, and again it's a leap of faith, an inference, an invitation to guess, that the perpetrators had a murderous intent. So as far as the murders are concerned we say that, with two exceptions which I'll come to, there is no evidence that the deaths in question were even caused by any single, identifiable perpetrator with the requisite mens rea, that as regards those exceptions there is no evidence at all that the perpetrators were Oric's subordinates and that there is absolutely no evidence that Oric ever knew or had specific information from which he could conclude that his subordinates, and I insist on that, that his subordinates committed murder. And that therefore it is deeply wrong and unfair for Oric to have to respond to charges of murder when the bare ingredients have not been met. Now to deal briefly with the charges of murder, as we've seen with Kukic, we agree that there is evidence that he was killed and that he was killed by Kemo. There is some evidence. We do not say how credible it is or where it leads. But firstly, arguably, it was caused when Kemo lost his self control after an act of provocation and that neither death or serious injury was intended, in which case, it is not murder. And the next slide, 32.1, sets out the facts as recalled by Nedjeljko Radic. I won't go over them, Your Honours will be familiar with the evidence, but it's -- it's simply set out there. In conclusion of -- to which I posed the question, "Did you get the impression from all this that Kemo didn't mean to kill Kukic." He answered: "I couldn't answer that. Probably not. If he'd known this blow would kill him he probably wouldn't, although I'm not sure. I don't know, really. I don't think -- I can't believe he was inhuman enough to kill a man. Only Kemo knows for sure." We haven't heard from Kemo, but in the U.K., certainly in many other jurisdictions, those facts could lead to manslaughter based on provocation or diminished responsibility. In many states in the US it would not be first degree murder. I don't make a big point of the provocation point because obviously it's not the -- the facts are not very sympathetic to that as a defence. But Your Honours have to, of course, be very careful at this stage not to allow charges to go forward on murder when it is quite possible that no question of murder even on the level of subordinate arises. In other words no evidence that a murder was committed. But then secondarily there was no evidence that Kemo was a subordinate of Oric. On the contrary, Dr. Mujkanovic affirmed that Kemo was not under Oric's control or anybody's control. Hakija Meholjic didn't know what unit Kemo was in, if he was in any. All that we know for sure from the Prosecution evidence is that Kemo was from Pale and we know from documents that there was an Independents Pale Battalion. We can rapidly review this evidence. There on slide 33.1, Dr. Mujkanovic refers to Kemo from Pale, "Was he a soldier or civilian?" "I can't say whether he held any function, I don't believe so." And then further, I think it's slide 33.2, he agreed that there were a number of individuals like Kemo who were out of control and he expressed an opinion that if Naser Oric tried to control Kemo, Kemo probably would have killed him, confirmed that 100 per cent.
