Then in answer to Your Honour's questions, slide 33.3 he said "Kemo didn't belong to anyone." And then slide 33.4, "No one could have sent Kemo anywhere. Kemo only belonged to himself, Mr. President." So therefore the only affirmative Prosecution evidence on Kemo is that he was emphatically not under the effective control of Naser Oric and therefore he cannot be considered a subordinate of Naser Oric under Article 7(3). Hakija Meholjic was asked about Kemo but he wasn't even sure if he was a soldier and he said "I don't know which unit he belonged to." That's slide 34.1. He's from Pale. He agreed that much. "Was he during the war, 92, 93, a fighter, Muslim fighter, soldier, whatever." "As far as I know he was." So he wasn't even entirely sure on that point. "Do you know which unit or formation or grouping or organisation of soldiers or fighters he was in?" "I don't know." And that's the fact. He didn't know. He then went on to speculate, "If he belonged to anybody, he belonged to the Potocari unit and who his commander was, I don't know." Hakija Meholjic also agreed that people did not necessarily belong to the units in their villages. And as I say the -- in fact, the only solid evidence which we have is that Kemo was from Pale and Exhibit D298 was, commented upon by General Sead Delic, confirmed that there was an Independent Pale Battalion who was not within any TO. Then we move on to the question of knowledge regarding the killing of Kukic and the Prosecution evidence was that Kemo immediately covered up the killing of Kukic by removing the body from the SUP and disposing of it in some unknown location and then making it clear to the prisoners that they were to keep it a secret and I'm looking at Radic's testimony 14th of January 2005, pages 23 to 25. So there is no evidence with regard to Kukic's killing that Naser Oric was informed of a murder, or even a possible murder, much less one committed by his subordinates. In fact, there was even evidence that the person allegedly Naser Oric had said, "Why didn't you tell us that Kukic was ill? We would have arrange for a doctor." So yes there was evidence that Kukic was killed but it's not clear that Kemo had the requisite mens rea, there was no evidence that Kemo was a subordinate of Naser Oric. And a fortiori there was no proof, no evidence that Oric knew that a subordinate of his had committed that crime, and that's in fact the death of Kukic, pretty much the only murder charged for which any evidence has been brought of the details of the actual death. If we turn to Jakov Dzokic, Jakov Dzokic's father testified that he had not seen his son. Okay. He may well be dead, but that does into the mean that he died in prison in Srebrenica between the 6th of February and 20th of March 1993, as alleged in the indictment. No one testified that Dzokic died in the prison. C007 last saw him alive in the prison. And in fact Ilija Ivanovic testified that he had heard that Dzokic was alive and had not died in the prison, and that's slide 36. In answer to a question he said, "I heard specifically that he was alive but I'd really like to know that he is. I heard he was thrown out of Srebrenica by the Muslim defenders." Even if Dzokic did die, there is no proof that Dzokic's death was the result of murder and again neither Prosecution nor Your Honours can just draw the inference least favourable to the accused namely that he died as a result of mistreatment in Srebrenica and that it was murder rather than death as a result of, say, neglect. And so surely you will not allow a case to go forward against Oric on charges of the murder of Dzokic, charges that Naser Oric is responsible for the murder of Dzokic, a terribly serious charge, as a result of making guess after guess about the facts of how Dzokic died, if he did die. That's surely deeply unjust. And again, no proof exists whatsoever that if Dzokic was murdered, it was by Oric's subordinates. And to avoid repeating that, that's true of all of the alleged murder victims. There is no proof that they were murdered rather than unlawfully killed with something less than the mens rea of murder, absolutely no proof that the individuals who inflicted mistreatment on these individuals were Oric's subordinates, people over whom he exercised effective control. In fact all the evidence has been that people from outside the prison came in and beat people. And again --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Have you incidentally on this alleged murder, looked at the evidence of Andja Radovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, she claimed that she was informed by C007 that he had died, but C007 didn't confirm that when he gave evidence. I have considered that, thank you, Your Honour. So I would again invite Your Honours to pose these questions for the Prosecution. How did they say are these people who did the beatings and murders? And if they don't know, if they can't say who those people are, how on earth can they say that they were Naser Oric's subordinates? Dragan Ilic, yes, there was testimony that he died in the prison, but again, as regards the actus reus of causing death, an element of murder is that the act or omissions by the accused's subordinates have to be a substantial cause of the death of the person. We know that the people who came from Cerska, Dragan Ilic and Branko Sekulic, were in very bad shape when they arrived in Srebrenica, so much so that C007 testified that it would not have surprised him if they had died on the way to Srebrenica. So if they did die in prison there was every possibility that their deaths were mostly caused from what they had suffered already, combined with the lack of food and disease which was rife in Srebrenica and from which everyone suffered. As far as the mens rea is concerned for the murder of Dragan Ilic, we don't know anything about who beat Ilic and what their mens rea was, and the perpetrator of any fatal beating of Ilic being completely unknown, there is no evidence whatsoever, yet again, that he was a subordinate of Oric. And a fortiari there is no evidence that Oric knew specifically anything of Ilic's murder by his subordinates. Mico Milovanovic. There was evidence that he in fact died in Glogova on the 24th of December 1992, and not in Srebrenica at all. That's D45 and D172. The fact that his wife hasn't seen him doesn't mean that he died in custody in Srebrenica. As far as how Mico, if it is indeed Mico Milovanovic, died, there is evidence of a Mico who died after being beaten by a young man, 16 to 20 years old. But there is nothing linking that beating with Mico Milovanovic and as far as the actus reus and mens rea of murder are concerned, there is no proof that the beating by this young man was the substantial cause of the death of Mico. In fact, he died a couple of says afterwards, or that it was done with the intent to kill, bearing in mind that this person was very young, may not have even been capable of forming the requisite intent. And again, no proof whatsoever that this very young man was a subordinate to Naser Oric. Civilian from Sase. And again, I -- I -- I come back time and again to this theme that the Prosecution is going to invite to you make huge leaps in every one of these cases, to assume that any death was a murder, that the persons who committed it from subordinates of Oric. Bogdan Zivanovic, I will refrain from passing any comment on and await to hear from the Prosecution what they say, why they say there is a case to answer. Turning to cruel treatment, Article 7(3) responsibility for cruel treatment, the position as far as that is concerned is the following: Yes, the evidence is that people were beaten, badly beaten, and that's obviously appalling and regrettable. But again we say there is insufficient evidence for the case to go forward on cruel treatment under Article 7(3). The evidence has not even made out a prima facie case that Oric's subordinates committed the crimes, much less that he knew or had specific information that his subordinates committed the crimes. That's where I come to in the skeleton point 9(A), and this point obviously applies to the murders as well but it's crucial the non-identification of the perpetrators of beatings. I make six points in that regard. Firstly a point I've made briefly, but that Article 7(3) is already a form of vicarious liability which has to be handled very carefully. It requires that Your Honours be sure that crimes were committed by the -- by subordinates with the necessary mens rea and actus reus. There are questions as to who the guards in the two facilities, detention facilities, were but this is a different question altogether from that of who beat and killed detainees because the evidence has been the guards did not beat detainees and that people came from outside the prison to do so. There was also a crucial distinction between visitors to the detention facilities, unless visitors, persons who visited the detention facilities, also beat people, the fact that the persons visited the prison doesn't begin to answer the question of who committed the crimes charged in the indictment. There is also a distinction between the people who arrested victims, and those who subsequently detained them. There is no chain of custody when it comes to persons who were in detention. One can be arrested by the metropolitan police and then delivered to Wandsworth prison. The two are different authorities and it's not an answer to the question of who committed beatings or who is responsible for beatings to point to who arrested or first detained a victim. And equally, and for the same reason, the bodies involved in the exchange of prisoners is not identical with the authority who detained the prisoners. In fact, the Prosecution itself expressly made that point at one stage when Ms. Richardson said, there was an objection, "my objection is being in charge of the prison is one thing, being in charge of the prisoner is something else." These are all subtle but important distinctions which Your Honours have to bear in mind. One can't simply conflate all these issues together and say, well, there is evidence that people were mistreated, there is evidence of another nature linking someone vaguely to something to do with the prisoners, therefore there is a case to answer. That's clearly insufficient. And finally, and I would reiterate for the final time, Naser Oric has to be shown to know or have specific information that his subordinates beat or killed people, and that has quite simply not been shown and that ultimately, among other reasons, is why the case must be thrown out on the detention charges. I would like to conclude, now, Your Honours, by making this observation, that the Prosecution's case so far has been based on multiple suppositions, if you like, that -- or at least for the case to go forward, that they will have to invite you to make suppositions of a nature that this person might have committed the crime, and if he did the crime, he might be a subordinate, and if he did the crime and if he's a subordinate, then it might be that Oric should have known that this had occurred, and it goes on and on. It's a bit like in mathematics, if one multiplies half by half by half by half, pretty son you have a one in 64 chance that an accused is responsible for a crime. That's very far from beyond a reasonable doubt. It's also very far from being enough for this case to go forward beyond the Prosecution case. It's no basis to allow a case to go forward, to heap supposition upon supposition. The Prosecution must be forced today's provide hard or to point to hard facts, concrete evidence, which actually makes out a case which can go forward. And Your Honours have a right to ask for that of the Prosecution. There is a very final word. There are many issues which we have not had the opportunity -- well, which we will not address at this stage because it's simply not a closing speech. But one thing we have not addressed is the situation as presented through Prosecution evidence that Naser Oric faced as a 25, 26 year old commander, and in that regard I just want to make two closing observations. First I want to recall what Dr. Mujkanovic said about the situation in Srebrenica at the time of the indictment, and it's slide 37. "If ever was hell on earth it must have been Srebrenica in 1992 and 1993. And as you know, 1993, 1994, 1995, were in actual fact something that bring shame to our civilisation, it was a time of famine, a time of daily attacks, daily shellings, poverty, with refugees flooding in from the general area." And then describing the situation of a commander in that situation, Colonel Tucker spoke of what this must have been like for a 25, 26 year old Naser Oric. It's slide number 38, and I'll read that in full. "The people there, particularly the refugees, they believed they were going to die. As I have described previously, it was not a question of if, it was only a question of when. Against this background, yes, there was a hero Naser Oric, but he had very few weapons, he had very few soldiers. The Serbs had many weapons, the Serbs had many soldiers, they didn't believe that he would actually be able to help them and defend them, but they believed he was doing his best." And I asked, as a military commander what that would be like to bear, and Colonel Tucker replied "He was operating in a most adverse and most difficult of circumstances and I cannot imagine having to operate in such circumstances." End quote. In this context and given the paucity of evidence against Naser Oric we say it is very regrettable, to say the least, that this case has been brought and that it has got this far. I genuinely do not see how it can be said that there is a case to answer. As I said in my opening speech, in our view, Oric's only crime was to decide that he would rather die fighting the Serbs than to flee from their genocidal onslaught, and they've never forgiven him for that. And I would just end on this quote, which is the following: "They chose to die in freedom rather than cower before an overpowering enemy. They refused to surrender, preferring to fight to the death and thus preserve their honour even when they could no longer defend their lives." And that was describing the Warsaw Jews who is were killed in the Warsaw Ghetto uprising in April/May 1943. We implore you to end this case now, unless I can assist you further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Jones. Perhaps you could tell us whether you have any submissions with regard to the killing of pigs in the context of this search for food.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Those were given to the Serb families in Srebrenica, I believe, was the evidence of Hakija Meholjic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, but that's -- I wonder, Hakija Meholjic ...

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I have no submissions on that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think he didn't -- they weren't killed in the case of Hakija Meholjic. They weren't killed on the spot. They were taken to Srebrenica and then given to the Serbs. Okay. With regard to other things that there is evidence about, having been taken by, I wouldn't say whether it's civilians or soldiers, I will leave that open, of course, which were not military hardware, that is not weapons, not arms, not ammunition, and not food and not clothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Households goods, for example, like --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: By civilians, well, Your Honour, the evidence was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If you have any submissions --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- because obviously I cannot --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- force to you make submissions.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: No. I have two submissions within that regard, that the evidence of Dr. Mujkanovic was that even household items which were taken, were taken so that they could be exchanged for food. And so still the idea was to obtain food to survive. As far as war booty is concerned, I would submit that it's -- it's broader than simply arms and ammunition. I did have an extract from the U.K. manual regarding war booty which actually enlarges the concept more broadly so that it includes even papers and various other matters. It's probably too elaborate to go into it now, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, I don't think it's --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: -- I would submit that war booty would be included. And another matter which again I would probably reserve for later, but is that there is evidence, too, that the Serb army had actually requisitioned whole areas for their use and that in those circumstances for -- of the fighters from Srebrenica to make use of those provisions requisitioned for the enemy means that that, too, fall -- would fall within war booty. In other words, if the enemy says everything here is for the use of our army, you're entitled to take that from them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. So more or less that brings the submissions of the Defence to an end. You will start tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You will start tomorrow. You will have the entire sitting, except that we would ask you to leave possibly the last half hour or so in case we need to come back to you on certain -- certain matters. And that particularly to you, having heard your submissions. But after your submissions, we may also need to go back to see whether the Defence have any comments to make. All right?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you, we will aim for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, and we stand adjourned until tomorrow morning at 9.00. We will make a last-ditch attempt to see if we can change the courtroom. However, please do believe me that we really tried hard and also please try again to see if we could -- we could possibly at that Trial Chamber I -- sorry, Courtroom I because Courtroom III seems to be more difficult. All right? Thank you. Yes, Ms. Sellers. Do you want to say anything?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: No, I'm standing up because --

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: It's in full respect, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
